title: Guru Tegh Bahadur's bani close

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhog, and your line: read for the departed. Today we close a whole stretch: thirty-two days with the ninth Guru.

If you had to describe a teacher in four words after a month with them, what would you pick? Not their biography. The feel of them: the voice you'd hear in your head when you needed it. We started this block on the ninth Guru's voice, calm and plain. Since then we've walked through his shabads in their ragas and all fifty-seven saloks. A wall of sand. Friends in good times. Kanchan. Fear none, frighten none. Auadh. Rama gone, Ravana gone. Strength gone, strength returned. Rahio. Before we turn to the Ardas, four words for the whole of it.
screen: `FOUR WORDS FOR A TEACHER.` → `A MONTH WITH THE NINTH GURU.` → `BEFORE WE TURN TO THE ARDAS.`

segments.voice: The four words are calm, fearless, detached, and kind. Calm. His bani has almost no drama in it. Short lines, plain words, the same truths said again and again: live in the world, shining, like a dream, auadh. It reads like someone speaking slowly to a friend who is upset. Fearless. The salok we met as fear none, frighten none says, in paraphrase, that the wise one gives fear to no one, and accepts fear from no one. Sikhs see that line lived out in his death. Tradition remembers that he went to Delhi and gave his life in 1675, and Sikhs honor him as having died for others' freedom to practice their own faith. He's often called Hind di chadar, the shield of India. Detached. The word in his bani is often bairaag, a turning away from clutching, and the picture is kanchan and iron alike, praise and blame alike. Not cold, but unhooked: love without clutching, as one day's line had it. Kind. This one is easy to miss, because his bani talks so much about death. But all that talk of passing is never meant to frighten. It's said the way you'd tell someone you love: we don't have forever, so let's not waste it. Strength gone, then strength returned. All companions gone, then rahio. Every hard line turns, sooner or later, toward what stays. That's the ninth Guru's bani: fifty-nine shabads in fifteen ragas, and fifty-seven saloks, most of them two lines long. Small in size. Not small in weight.
screen: `CALM: PLAIN LINES, SAID SLOWLY.` · `FEARLESS: FEAR NONE, FRIGHTEN NONE.` · `DETACHED: GOLD AND IRON ALIKE.` · `KIND: EVERY HARD LINE TURNS.` · then, large: `CALM AND FEARLESS.`

segments.voice: Let a few of this month's lines pass through your mind: live in the world, shining; like a dream; nothing stays; today or tomorrow; only you; the Name remains; nothing equals it. Don't choose the wisest; notice the one that tugs, and say it three times, slowly, with your breath. If you pray, follow it with Waheguru.
Nirbhau, without fear. One of four words for his bani: calm, nirbhau, detached, and kind: fifty-nine shabads and fifty-seven saloks, small in size, not small in weight.
Your line: calm and fearless. Tomorrow, the prayer said standing. Day six hundred ten, and a whole block done.

howItsDone: Sikhs hear Guru Tegh Bahadur's shabads in kirtan and his saloks at every bhog, and on the day of his martyrdom, often observed in November or December, gurdwaras sing his bani and tell the story of Delhi.
